issues.legal_issue: A special expedited eviction procedure for landlords seeking possession for specified personal housing needs does not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality.
material_facts: The eviction proceedings concerned a landlord seeking possession for personal bona fide need under a category covered by the special procedure.
The ordinary eviction process could take years, during which the landlord might die or the need for possession might disappear.
The special procedure provided for a tenant to obtain leave to defend before contesting the eviction claim.
issues.conclusion: The special procedure was enacted in the public interest and did not violate Article 14 because the class of landlords receiving its benefit had a reasonable connection to the legislation’s purpose.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits the legislature to create a class of landlords for a special procedure where the classification has a reasonable nexus with the law’s object. The Court relied on Kewal Singh v. Lajwanti, Sarwan Singh v. Kasturi Lal, and Vinod Kumar Chowdhry v. Narain Devi Taneja in upholding the special procedure and its classification.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_special_evic: A party challenges the constitutional validity of a special procedure for eviction proceedings.
predicates.landlord_seeks_possession_for_personal_h: The landlord seeks possession of the premises for a qualifying personal housing need.
predicates.ordinary_process_causes_prolonged_delay: The ordinary process for resolving the eviction claim may take so long that the landlord’s need may disappear or the landlord may die before obtaining relief.
predicates.special_procedure_has_a_reasonable_conne: The special procedure is designed to provide landlords with qualifying needs more timely relief.

issues.definition: When a special eviction procedure is challenged, it is constitutional if it addresses qualifying personal housing needs, the ordinary process causes prolonged delay, and the special procedure is reasonably connected to providing speedy relief.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord proceeding under the special rent-control procedure for a qualifying eviction need not first obtain permission under the slum-area legislation, even when the premises are in a slum area.
material_facts: The premises were within a designated slum area.
The landlord had previously sought permission to institute eviction proceedings under the slum-area legislation, but permission was refused and the refusal was upheld on appeal.
The landlord later brought an eviction proceeding under the special rent-control procedure for a qualifying personal need.
The special rent-control provisions contained a non-obstante clause and were enacted after the relevant slum-area provisions.
issues.conclusion: The special rent-control procedure overrides inconsistent requirements of the slum-area legislation, so prior permission from the competent authority was not required for the eviction proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the non-obstante provisions in sections 14A and 25A–25C of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, and held that the later special procedure prevails over inconsistent provisions, including section 19 of the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956. It relied on Sarwan Singh v. Kasturi Lal, Kewal Singh v. Lajwanti, and Vinod Kumar Chowdhry v. Narain Devi Taneja, and approved Smt. Krishna Devi Nigam v. Shyam Babu Gupta.

predicates.eviction_proceeding_under_special_rent_p: The landlord brings an eviction proceeding under a special procedure for a qualifying ground of eviction.
predicates.premises_are_in_a_slum_area: The premises are located in an area subject to a statutory slum-area regime.
predicates.special_procedure_conflicts_with_prior_p: The special eviction procedure conflicts with a requirement to obtain prior permission under another law.

issues.definition: If an eviction proceeding uses the special rent procedure for a qualifying ground, concerns premises in a slum area, and conflicts with a prior-permission requirement, the landlord need not obtain that permission.

issues.legal_issue: The special eviction procedure applies on the same principle to qualifying proceedings based on personal need and to proceedings under the separate landlord-occupation category.
material_facts: The eviction proceeding was brought under the personal-need ground and the special procedure.
The tenants argued that the separate landlord-occupation category justified a special procedure, but the personal-need ground did not.
The Court held that the distinction between the two categories did not warrant different treatment for purposes of the special procedure.
issues.conclusion: There was no difference in principle or law between the two categories that would prevent the special procedure from applying to the personal-need ground.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 14(1)(e), 14A, and 25A–25C of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, form part of a special scheme for specified landlord eviction claims. The Court relied on Sarwan Singh v. Kasturi Lal and Kewal Singh v. Lajwanti in rejecting the proposed distinction between the categories.

predicates.eviction_proceeding_under_special_rent_p: The landlord brings an eviction proceeding under the statutory special procedure.
predicates.claim_falls_within_personal_need_or_land: The eviction claim is based on either a qualifying personal housing need or a qualifying landlord-occupation circumstance.

issues.definition: A claim based on either qualifying personal housing need or qualifying landlord occupation falls within the special eviction procedure when the proceeding is brought under that procedure.
